newsitem.title: UK: Peru's Fujimori sees hostage talks on Tuesday.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Fujimori sees hostage talks on Tuesday.

text.p: Peru's President Alberto Fujimori said on Sunday he hoped to restart preliminary talks next week with Marxist guerrillas holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home in the Peruvian capital.

As he arrived in London for a conference designed to boost British investment in Latin America, Fujimori told Reuters everything was set for talks to go ahead and he was optimistic the two-month crisis could be solved without bloodshed.
"The talks, that we have described as preliminary, will probably start next Tuesday... and continue until we can start definitive negotiations," Fujimori said in an interview.

However, the MRTA has said it will not start talks with the government unless Fujimori drops his refusal to talk about their main demand, which is to free some 400 jailed comrades. Fujimori gave no details of how he expected the talks to go ahead.
In Lima, security forces have been preparing a house opposite the residence for use in any eventual talks.
He added: "We will exhaust all possible avenues to ensure that the hostages are freed without the use of force."
The heavily armed MRTA guerrillas stormed the residence on December 17, seizing hundreds of cocktail-party guests.
Most have now been freed, but the Japanese and Bolivian envoys, as well as local and Japanese businessmen, and Fujimori's brother, Pedro, are still being held.
Concern is mounting about the health of some of the hostages and the Red Cross has arranged medical visits by specialists.
Fujimori has refused to discuss the rebels' demand for the release of their comrades.
But last weekend in Canada, Fujimori promised Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto he would try and resume dialogue between the rebels and the government broken off on December 28.

Government sources have said Fujimori might travel to Romania after Britain, sparking speculation that the East European country could figure in an asylum deal for the 15 MRTA rebels in the residence, who are led by Nestor Cerpa Cartolini.
But Fujimori said there was no asylum deal set up.
"We haven't had success finding a country where they could seek asylum. It is quite a complex situation and in this moment there are few countries willing to have them," Fujimori said.
Security around the residence is tight, with sharpshooters backed up by armoured personnel carriers around the building and local residents being issued with identity cards.

Security forces have also continued psychological warfare to wear the rebels down, blasting the residence with patriotic "criolla" folk music from huge speakers. The rebels have answered back by chanting revolutionary hymns and slogans.
As Fujimori was speaking, news came through of a bomb attack by suspected Maoist Shining Path guerrillas on an electric power company on the outskirts of the Peruvian capital of Lima.
Windows were shattered, but there were no reports of injuries or deaths. Fujimori said he was awaiting more details.
But he dismissed reports in neighbouring Ecuador that Peruvian troops were moving towards the disputed border.

"There is no movement of troops on either side of the border. We are in a process of negotiation... In these circumstances the movement of troops is hardly likely. Let us hope it never happens," said Fujimori.
Fujimori has voiced "deep concern" about the constitutional crisis in Ecuador following the decision by that country's Congress to oust President Abdala Bucaram.
He has also agreed to postpone talks over the border dispute between the two countries until after the crisis is resolved.

The border dispute erupted in a brief but bloody war in early 1995 that left dozens dead and hundreds injured on both sides. The two countries are due to hold talks in Brazil to try and end the 55-year-old dispute. REUTER APM
